newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin denounces French hand in Holocaust.
newsitem.headline: Jospin denounces French hand in Holocaust.

text.p: Prime Minister Lionel Jospin denounced on Sunday the French state's responsibility in the Holocaust and in anti-Jewish repression during Nazi occupation.

Echoing remarks made by Gaullist President Jacques Chirac at the same ceremony two years ago, Socialist Jospin marked the 55th anniversary of the 'Vel D'Hiv' swoop in which 13,000 Jews were arrested and sent to death camps in July 1942.

"July 16 and 17, 1942, are in the history of our country a mark of infamy," Jospin, appointed prime minister after a leftist win in a parliamentary election on June 1, said in a speech at a monument to Jewish martyrs built on the site of the cycling track where deportees were gathered.

"This roundup was decided, planned and carried out by Frenchmen. Political leaders, administrators, judges, policemen, gendarmes took part in it," Jospin said. "Not one German soldier was needed for this infamy."
But the premier stressed a distinction between the collaborationist Vichy regime and the French Republic.
"To recall (this infamy), cruel and revolting as it was, does not lead us to confuse the Vichy regime and the Republic, the collaborators and the Resistance fighters, the prudent and the just.
"We must only recognise, as did President Chirac two years ago, that a government, an administration of our country, committed the irreparable."

In an explicit reference to the trial of former cabinet minister Maurice Papon for alleged war crimes starting on October 6, Jospin said that France must "answer the desire for justice" in memory of the victims.

Papon is charged with crimes against humanity for sending 1,560 Jews, including many children, on their way to death camps in 1942-44 from Bordeaux where he was secretary-general of the Vichy prefect's office.

"The duty of remembrance demands that those on whom weighs suspicion of responsibility in past crimes be tried. It is important that what was not done yesterday be done today, without waiting any longer," Jospin said.

In 1995, Chirac had acknowledged that the Nazis' "criminal folly" had been seconded by French nationals and by the French State, an admission which his predecessor Francois Mitterrand, France's first Socialist President, had always refused to make.
The late Mitterrand, who served as a Vichy official and in the Resistance, sought to prevent trials for crimes against humanity, arguing they undermined national unity.
"We owe France's Jewish deportees an imprescriptible debt," Chirac had said.
Mitterrand unveiled the monument to Jewish martyrs in 1994 but refused to "make amends in the name of France" and the Republic, on the grounds, he said, that the Vichy authorities were illegal.
